conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time today. I’m Dr. Marin, a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with pregnancy, birth, and new motherhood. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, and it helps us see whether you might benefit from extra support or resources. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, so please feel free to speak openly. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about “right” or “wrong” answers. Ready to start?

1. Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

[pauses, gives a small shrug]  
I guess… I still laugh sometimes, like when my sister sends me those silly memes. But mostly I feel like I’m faking it. Things that used to crack me up—my husband’s dumb jokes, even the baby’s funny faces—just feel kind of flat. It’s like the laugh doesn’t reach all the way inside me anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, I suppose, but it doesn’t come as easy. Most of the time I feel like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[eyes drop to my lap, voice quiet]

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little things—coffee with a friend, even just getting out of the house—but when the time comes it feels like more effort than it’s worth. I still do them, but the “looking-forward-to-it” part feels kind of… hollow.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[lightly twisting the edge of my sleeve]

Sometimes, yeah… like if the baby’s extra fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I’ll replay every little choice—did I eat something that upset her, did I pick her up too fast? It’s not every minute, but a couple of times this week I caught myself thinking she’d settle better if I just “knew what I was doing.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I’ve definitely been on edge, mostly about the baby. Like, I’ll lie down and suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds normal, or I’ll check the monitor three times because I’m scared the swaddle slipped over her face. I know it’s probably fine, but the worry just shows up—tight chest, can’t settle—even when nothing’s actually wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods slowly, eyes a little wide]

Yeah… a couple of nights this week I’d be feeding her in the dark and out of nowhere my heart starts racing, like something awful is about to happen. I couldn’t name what—I know we’re safe in the house, door’s locked, baby’s okay—but I’d feel shaky and have to grip the chair arms until it passed. It’s scary enough that I hate being alone when it hits.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]

Yes… most days. I’ll be folding laundry while she naps and suddenly feel like the pile is endless, like no matter how much I do there’s always bottles to wash, diapers to change, me still in the same milk-stained shirt. I keep telling myself millions of moms handle this, but sometimes it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff and can’t come up for air.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but yeah—some evenings I finally get her down, crawl into bed exhausted, and then my brain just…won’t shut off. I replay every cry, every feeding, worry she’ll wake up any second, or I picture worst-case stuff. I lie there staring at the ceiling until the monitor lights up with her first stretchy whimper and I feel like I barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shrugs, voice small]

Yeah… I do feel sad off and on. It’s not all day, but little waves hit—like when I’m rocking her and suddenly feel lonely even though she’s right there. I’ll tear up for no clear reason, then feel silly because I’ve got this healthy baby. The sadness slips in, then slips away, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, eyes glassy]

Not every day… but a couple of times. Yesterday I finally got her to nap and I sat on the couch and just started crying—quiet, so no one would hear. I couldn’t even say why. It felt like all the tired and worry just spilled out. Then I wiped my face, told myself to pull it together, and went to fold more onesies.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I get overwhelmed, sure, but I would never want to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for her. I just want to feel better, not disappear.

You've shared that the joy and laughter that once came easily now feel distant, replaced by waves of sadness, self-doubt, and near-nightly worry about your baby's safety. Even simple tasks like folding laundry can feel overwhelming, and you've found yourself quietly crying when the house is finally still. You love your daughter fiercely and want to be the best mom possible, yet much of the time you feel as though you're simply "going through the motions" rather than truly living.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 20, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished anticipatory pleasure—describes the feeling as "hollow" and effortful—aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a couple of times this week" and gives examples of unnecessary guilt, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about the baby's safety that occur without objective cause and trigger physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (racing heart, shaking) occurring multiple times this week without identifiable cause, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up with daily tasks, and uses metaphor of drowning, matching "Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sleep-interfering rumination and worry several nights per week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>recurring "little waves" of sadness that "keep coming back"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying episodes a couple of times in the past week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 20 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale falls well above the 14-point threshold indicating a high probability of major <med>depression</med> with <med>peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses diminished pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), persistent self-blame, frequent anxiety/panic not tied to real threats, middle-of-the-night rumination, and repeated crying spells-symptoms that align with DSM-5 criteria for a major depressive episode. Because she also describes sudden heart-racing episodes, comorbid <med>anxiety</med> is likely. Absence of self-harm ideation (Item 10 = 0) lowers immediate safety risk but does not negate the need for urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Begin tracking mood, sleep hours, and panic episodes to share at your visit
3. Accept help with overnight feeds or household tasks to protect 4- to 5-hour stretches of rest
4. Practice 5-minute paced breathing or grounding exercises when panic rises; consider a free app for guidance
5. Share this EPDS result with a trusted family member so they can support follow-through with care
6. If feelings suddenly worsen or you develop thoughts of self-harm, seek emergency care or call 988 (U.S.)
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient: Postpartum mother (infant < 1 yr)
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed
- Anhedonia, reduced pleasure (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)
- Persistent worry, intrusive “what-if” re infant safety, nocturnal panic episodes (Q4, Q5)
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning” in daily tasks (Q6)
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to rumination (Q7)
- Sad/miserable mood with tearfulness; crying spells 2× this week (Q8, Q9)
- No self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern
Low mood plus prominent anxiety/panic; functional impact on sleep, enjoyment, and coping.

Screening significance
EPDS equivalent items: #1, #2, #3, #4, #5, #6, #7, #8, #9 positive; #10 negative.
Meets threshold for probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; no acute safety concern.

Risk factors noted
Primiparous, high self-expectations, limited support expression, sleep deprivation.

Plan
Provide EPDS for completion; discuss further assessment for depression and anxiety; review supports and safety plan.
